trappan.prompt: Work out the division with long division.
mul.prompt: Set up the multiplication in columns and work it out.
mul.promptDecimals: Make the numbers whole, work it out – and put the decimals back at the end.
teori.mul.multiplicationTwoDigit.1: Let's work out 23 · 14. Write the numbers with the ones under each other. You make one row for each digit of 14.
teori.mul.multiplicationTwoDigit.2: First the ones digit 4: 4 · 3 = 12, write 2 and carry 1. Then 4 · 2 = 8, plus 1 is 9. The first row is 92.
teori.mul.multiplicationTwoDigit.3: Now the tens digit 1. It's worth 10, so the row starts one step to the left – under the 1. 1 · 3 = 3 and 1 · 2 = 2. The row is 23 tens, that is 230.
teori.mul.multiplicationTwoDigit.4: Now the rows are added. Write a plus sign in front of the last row.
teori.mul.multiplicationTwoDigit.5: Add the rows as usual, from the ones: 92 + 230 = 322. So 23 · 14 = 322.
teori.mul.multiplicationTwoDigit.6: Common mistake: forgetting to move the second row one step left. Then you count 23 instead of 230.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimal.1: Let's work out 3.4 · 6. Make 3.4 a whole number by taking away the point: it becomes 34. You took away one decimal – remember it.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimal.2: Work it out with the whole numbers as usual: 34 · 6 = 204.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimal.3: Put back the decimal you took away: the answer gets one digit after the point. 204 becomes 20.4.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimal.4: Took away two decimals? Then put back two. 1.25 · 3: 125 · 3 = 375, and two decimals back is 3.75.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimal.5: Common mistake: forgetting to put the decimal back. 3.4 · 6 isn't 204.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimalDecimal.1: Let's work out 0.2 · 0.03. Make both whole: 0.2 becomes 2 – one decimal away. 0.03 becomes 3 – two decimals away. In all 1 + 2 = 3 decimals.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimalDecimal.2: Work it out with the whole numbers: 2 · 3 = 6.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimalDecimal.3: Put the 3 decimals back: the answer gets 3 digits after the point. 6 has only one, so fill in zeros in front: 0.006.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimalDecimal.4: The same with 2.5 · 1.3: 25 · 13 = 325. One + one decimal = two back: 3.25.
teori.mul.multiplicationDecimalDecimal.5: Common mistake: putting back only one decimal. Count all you took away – in 0.2 · 0.03 it's three.
trappan.promptRest: Work out the division with long division. It doesn't go evenly – the answer is a whole number and a remainder.
teori.div.divisionRest.1: Sometimes a division doesn't go evenly. Then something is left over – a remainder. Let's work out 17 ÷ 5.
teori.div.divisionRest.2: 5 doesn't go into 1, so look at 17. 5 goes into 17 3 times, because 3 · 5 = 15 and 4 · 5 = 20 is too much.
teori.div.divisionRest.4: Subtract: 17 − 15 = 2. There are no more digits to bring down. 2 is the remainder – what was left over. The answer is 3 remainder 2.
teori.div.divisionRest.5: Check the answer: multiply back and add the remainder. 3 · 5 + 2 = 17. Correct!
teori.div.divisionRest.6: Common mistake: a remainder as big as the number you divide by, or bigger. 7 left when dividing by 5? Then 5 went in once more.
trappan.promptRound: Work out the division with long division and round the answer to {n} decimals.
trappan.promptRound1: Work out the division with long division and round the answer to one decimal.
trappan.shift: You're dividing by a decimal. Move the decimal point {n} places right in both numbers – then you divide by a whole number, and the answer stays the same:
teori.div.divisionTrappan.1: Let's work out 84 ÷ 4 with the bus stop. The number you divide by, 4, is on the left. 84 goes under the step. The answer is written above.
teori.div.divisionTrappan.2: Start with the first digit, 8. How many times does 4 go into 8? 2 times, because 2 · 4 = 8. Write 2 above the 8.
teori.div.divisionTrappan.5: Bring down the next digit, the 4, next to the zero. Now you have 4.
teori.div.divisionTrappan.6: The same steps again: 4 goes into 4 once. 1 · 4 = 4, and 4 − 4 = 0. The answer is 21. Remember the order: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
teori.div.divisionTrappan.7: Common mistake: skipping a zero. In 412 ÷ 4, 4 doesn't go into 1 – so you write 0 in the answer and bring down the next digit. The answer is 103, not 13.
teori.div.divisionTwoDigit.1: Now we divide by a two-digit number: 156 ÷ 12. First write out the 12 times table – then you don't have to guess.
teori.div.divisionTwoDigit.2: Does 12 go into 1? No, 1 is too small. Take two digits: 15. The table shows 1 · 12 = 12 fits, but 2 · 12 = 24 is too much. Write 1 above the 5.
teori.div.divisionTwoDigit.3: Multiply back: 1 · 12 = 12. Write 12 under 15 and subtract: 15 − 12 = 3.
teori.div.divisionTwoDigit.4: Bring down the 6. Now you have 36. In the table: 3 · 12 = 36. Write 3 in the answer.
teori.div.divisionTwoDigit.6: Common mistake: choosing too small. If what's left is as big as the number you divide by – or bigger – it fits once more. Try a bigger number.
teori.div.divisionDecimals.1: 9 ÷ 2 doesn't come out even. But with the bus stop you can carry on past the decimal comma and get an answer with decimals.
teori.div.divisionDecimals.2: 2 goes into 9 four times: 4 · 2 = 8, and 9 − 8 = 1. There's 1 left over – a remainder.
teori.div.divisionDecimals.3: 9 is the same as 9,0. Put a comma in the answer after the 4, and bring down a zero. Now you have 10.
teori.div.divisionDecimals.4: 2 goes into 10 five times: 5 · 2 = 10, and 10 − 10 = 0. The answer is 4,5.
teori.div.divisionDecimals.5: Common mistake: stopping at a remainder. 9 ÷ 2 isn't 4 – carry on with a zero after the comma.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDividend.1: 8,4 ÷ 4. Work it out just as usual, one digit at a time.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDividend.3: Now you bring down the 4 that's after the comma. So you put a comma in the answer – straight above the comma in 8,4. 4 goes into 4 once.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDividend.5: Common mistake: forgetting the comma in the answer. 12,6 ÷ 3 is 4,2 – not 42.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDivisor.1: Dividing by a decimal, like 0,3, is awkward. So we turn it into a whole number first.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDivisor.2: 0,3 has one decimal. Move the comma one step to the right in both numbers: 0,3 becomes 3, and 4,5 becomes 45.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDivisor.3: The answer stays the same, because both numbers became 10 times bigger.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDivisor.4: Now work out 45 ÷ 3 with the bus stop as usual. The answer is 15.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDivisor.5: If the number you divide by has two decimals, move the comma two steps in both: 0,12 becomes 12, and 2,46 becomes 246.
teori.div.divisionDecimalDivisor.6: Common mistake: moving the comma in only one of the numbers. Move it just as far in both.
teori.div.divisionRounding.1: Sometimes a division never ends – there is always a remainder left. Then work out one decimal more than you need, and round.

teori.placeValue.mistake: Common mistake: answering 5. The question is what the digit is worth – in the hundreds place the 5 is worth 500.
teori.additionBasic.mistake: Common mistake: mixing up the columns. Ones under ones, tens under tens – otherwise the answer is far too big.
teori.subtractionBasic.mistake: Common mistake: taking the top from the bottom. It's always the top number minus the bottom one.
teori.additionCarry.mistake: Common mistake: forgetting the carry. 47 + 38 then comes out as 75 instead of 85.
teori.subtractionBorrow.mistake: Common mistake: turning the numbers round and doing 7 − 2 in the ones. Then 52 − 27 comes out wrong: 35 instead of 25.
teori.subtractionZero.mistake: Common mistake: borrowing from a zero. A zero has nothing to give – move on to the left first.
teori.multiplicationBasic.mistake: Common mistake: multiplying only the ones. The tens get multiplied too: 23 · 3 = 69.
teori.multiplicationCarry.mistake: Common mistake: forgetting to add the carry after the next multiplication. 47 · 6 then comes out as 242 instead of 282.
teori.decimalColumn.mistake: Common mistake: lining the numbers up by their last digit. It's the decimal commas that go under each other.
teori.decimalColumn.4: Subtraction works the same way: comma under comma. 2 − 8 doesn't work, so you exchange as usual: 12 − 8 = 4. The answer is 3,4.
teori.decimalColumn.5: Do the numbers have different numbers of decimals? Fill out with a zero so they have the same: 3,5 is the same as 3,50.
teori.statisticsMean.mistake: Don't forget to divide! The sum 32 isn't the mean – divide by how many numbers there are: 32 / 4 = 8.
teori.statisticsMean.check: What is the mean of 2, 4 and 6?
teori.statisticsMedian.mistake: Common mistake: taking the middle number without sorting first. Always put the numbers in order.
teori.statisticsMedian.check: What is the median of 7, 1 and 4?
teori.statisticsMode.mistake: Common mistake: choosing the biggest number. The mode is the number that appears most often.
teori.statisticsMode.check: What is the mode of 3, 5, 3 and 8?
teori.chartReading.mistake: Common mistake: counting squares. Read the number on the scale where the bar ends.
teori.chartReading.check: How many does the bar show?
teori.adv.negativeNumbers.1: Negative numbers lie to the left of zero on the number line. −3 is three steps left of zero.
teori.adv.negativeNumbers.2: Taking away a negative number is the same as adding: minus a minus is plus.
teori.adv.negativeNumbers.3: Times: two negative numbers give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer.
teori.adv.negativeNumbers.4: Common mistake: −3 − 5 isn't −2. From −3 you go five steps left, to −8.
teori.adv.powers.1: A power is repeated multiplication. 2³ means 2 times itself three times.
teori.adv.powers.2: The exponent says how many times. 10³ is a one with three zeros: 1 000.
teori.adv.scientific.1: Big and small numbers are written shorter in scientific notation: a number from 1 to 10, times a power of ten.
teori.adv.scientific.2: Positive exponent: move the decimal comma that many steps to the right.
teori.adv.scientific.3: Negative exponent: move it to the left – the number becomes small.
teori.adv.scientific.4: Common mistake: 10³ isn't 30. It's three tens multiplied: 1 000.
teori.adv.percent.1: Percent means hundredths. 25 % is 25 squares out of 100 – a quarter.
teori.adv.percent.2: Write the percentage as a decimal and multiply: 25 % = 0.25.
teori.adv.percent.3: Common mistake: using 25 instead of 0.25. 25 % of 80 can never be more than 80.
teori.adv.changeFactor.1: If something goes up by 15 % it becomes 115 % of what it was. The change factor is 1.15.
teori.adv.changeFactor.2: New value = old value times the change factor.
teori.adv.changeFactor.3: If it goes down by 20 %, 80 % is left. The change factor is 0.80.
teori.adv.changeFactor.4: Common mistake: an increase of 5 % is 1.05 – not 1.5. That would be an increase of 50 %.
teori.adv.changeFactor.5: What change factor goes with a decrease of 10 %?
teori.adv.simplify.1: Terms with x can be added up, just like 3 apples + 2 apples = 5 apples.
teori.adv.simplify.2: Gather the x terms on their own and the numbers on their own.
teori.adv.simplify.3: Common mistake: 3x + 2 isn't 5x. An x term and a number can't be added together.
teori.adv.equations.1: An equation is like a balanced scale: both sides are worth the same.
teori.adv.equations.2: Do the same thing to both sides: take away 5, then divide by 3.
teori.adv.equations.3: Check your answer! Put x = 5 into the equation. If it holds, it's right.
teori.adv.equations.4: Common mistake: 3x means 3 times x. So you divide by 3 – you don't take away 3.
teori.adv.equationsBoth.1: When x is on both sides, we gather all the x's on one side.
teori.adv.equationsBoth.2: Take 2x away from both sides and add 3. Then solve as usual.
teori.adv.equationsBoth.3: Common mistake: forgetting to change the sign when a term moves across. +3 becomes −3 on the other side.
teori.adv.pythagoras.1: In a right triangle the longest side is called the hypotenuse (c). The other two are the legs (a and b).
teori.adv.pythagoras.2: Pythagoras' theorem: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the legs.
teori.adv.pythagoras.3: Work it out, and take the square root at the end.
teori.adv.pythagoras.4: Common mistake: c isn't a + b. Square first, add, then take the square root.
teori.adv.pythagoras.5: The legs are 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse?
teori.adv.linear.1: The equation of a straight line: y = kx + m. m is where the line crosses the y-axis, k is its slope.
teori.adv.linear.2: To get y, put the x value into the equation.
teori.adv.linear.3: The slope is the difference in y divided by the difference in x – how much y grows when x grows by 1.
teori.adv.linear.4: Common mistake: dividing the wrong way round. The y difference goes on top.
teori.adv.linear.5: y = 3x − 2. What is y when x = 2?
teori.adv.pq.1: A quadratic equation often has two solutions – where the curve crosses the x-axis.
teori.adv.pq.2: The pq formula. First the equation must be in the form x² + px + q = 0.
teori.adv.pq.3: Here p = 2 and q = −8. The solutions are x₁ = 2 and x₂ = −4.
teori.adv.pq.4: Common mistake: dropping the minus sign in front of p/2. It's always −p/2 first.
teori.adv.pq.5: What are the solutions of x² − 5x + 6 = 0?
teori.adv.logarithms.1: lg x answers the question: what must 10 be raised to, to make x?
teori.adv.logarithms.2: Powers of ten give whole answers.
teori.adv.logarithms.3: When x is in the exponent, you solve the equation with lg.
teori.adv.logarithms.4: Common mistake: lg isn't division by 10. lg 1 000 = 3, because 10³ = 1 000.
teori.adv.trigonometry.1: In a right triangle, each angle goes with ratios between the sides.
teori.adv.trigonometry.2: a is the leg opposite the angle v, b is the leg next to it, and c is the hypotenuse.
teori.adv.trigonometry.3: If you know c and v you can work out the side. sin 30° = 0.5.
teori.adv.trigonometry.4: Common mistake: mixing up the opposite and the adjacent leg. Always start from the angle.
teori.adv.derivative.1: The derivative f′(x) is the curve's slope at a point – how fast f is changing right there.
teori.adv.derivative.2: The rule: the exponent moves down in front, and the exponent goes down by 1.
teori.adv.derivative.3: Differentiate term by term. A constant like 5 has slope 0 and disappears.
teori.adv.derivative.4: Common mistake: forgetting to lower the exponent. The derivative of x³ is 3x².
teori.adv.integral.1: The integral from a to b is the area between the curve and the x-axis.
teori.adv.integral.2: Find an antiderivative F – differentiate backwards – and work out F(b) − F(a).
teori.adv.integral.3: 3x² has the antiderivative x³. Put in the limits.
teori.adv.integral.4: Common mistake: working out F(a) − F(b). It's the upper limit minus the lower one.
teori.adv.integral.5: What is the integral of 2x from 0 to 1?
expr.moreSolutions: Right so far! There are more solutions – can you find them?

geo.tip.1.2.1: The perimeter is the way all around the shape. Add up every side.
geo.tip.2.4.1: The area is base times height. A square's sides are all the same length. Perimeter: add up all four sides.
geo.tip.2.4.2: A triangle is half a rectangle: A = b · h / 2. The height is at right angles to the base.
geo.tip.2.4.3: A = b · h, where h is the height (the dashed line) – not the slanted side.
geo.tip.2.4.4: Split the shape into rectangles and triangles. Add what is there and take away what has been cut out.
geo.tip.3.4.3: d = 2r. The circumference is π · d and the area is π · r². Use π ≈ 3,14 and set the multiplication up in a column.
geo.tip.3.4.4: A = (a + b) · h / 2 – add the parallel sides, times the height, divided by two.
geo.tip.3.4.5: Work out each part on its own. A half circle is π · r² / 2. The radius is half the diameter.
geo.tip.3.4.6: Write the formula with the unknown number, put in what you know and solve for what is missing.
geo.tip.4.2.2: A sector of v degrees is v/360 of the circle – of both its area and its circumference.
geo.tip.4.2.3: T = a · b · sin C / 2, where C is the angle between the sides a and b.
teori.geo.perimeter.1: The perimeter is how far it is all the way round the shape – like walking once along its edge.
teori.geo.perimeter.2: Add up every side. A rectangle has four sides: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm.
teori.geo.perimeter.3: A triangle has three sides. Add up all three.
teori.geo.perimeter.4: Common mistake: counting only two of the sides. Go all the way round!
teori.geo.perimeter.5: Try it: a square has sides of 2 cm. How long is its perimeter?
teori.geo.rectangleArea.1: The area is how much surface the shape covers – how many 1 cm² squares fit inside.
teori.geo.rectangleArea.2: For a rectangle, the area is base times height: 5 · 3 = 15 cm².
teori.geo.rectangleArea.3: A square's sides are all equal, so its area is side times side.
teori.geo.rectangleArea.4: Common mistake: adding the sides. That gives the perimeter, not the area.
teori.geo.rectangleArea.5: Try it: a rectangle is 6 cm long and 2 cm high. What is its area?
teori.geo.triangleArea.1: A triangle is exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height.
teori.geo.triangleArea.2: So its area is base times height, divided by two.
teori.geo.triangleArea.3: The base is 6 cm and the height 4 cm: 6 · 4 / 2 = 12 cm².
teori.geo.triangleArea.4: Common mistake: forgetting to divide by two.
teori.geo.triangleArea.5: Try it: the base is 10 cm and the height 3 cm. What is the area?
teori.geo.parallelogram.1: A parallelogram is a rectangle pushed sideways. Its height is the dashed line.
teori.geo.parallelogram.2: The area is base times height: 7 · 4 = 28 cm².
teori.geo.parallelogram.3: Cut the triangle off one end and move it to the other – it becomes a rectangle, 7 long and 4 high.
teori.geo.parallelogram.4: Common mistake: using the slanted side instead of the height.
teori.geo.parallelogram.5: Try it: the base is 9 cm and the height 5 cm. What is the area?
teori.geo.compositeBasic.1: A composite shape is built from simpler shapes. Here, a rectangle with one corner cut away.
teori.geo.compositeBasic.2: Work out the area of the whole rectangle and of the piece that is gone.
teori.geo.compositeBasic.4: Common mistake: adding the piece instead of taking it away.
teori.geo.compositeBasic.5: Try it: a 10 by 4 rectangle with a triangle of base 4 and height 2 cut out. How much area is left?
teori.geo.circle.1: The radius r goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter d goes right across through the centre – twice as long.
teori.geo.circle.2: The circumference is π times the diameter, and the area is π times the radius squared. π is a number of about 3,14 – that's what you work with.
teori.geo.circle.3: The radius is 3 cm. The radius squared: 3 · 3 = 9. The area is π · 9 – so 3,14 · 9.
teori.geo.circle.4: Common mistake: putting the diameter into the area formula. It is the radius that is squared.
teori.geo.circle.5: Try it: the radius is 5 cm. How long is the circumference?
teori.geo.circle.decimals: 3,14 has two decimals, so the answer gets two decimals: 28,26. Rounded to one decimal: 28,3 cm².
teori.geo.trapezoid.1: A trapezoid has two parallel sides, a and b, and the height h between them.
teori.geo.trapezoid.2: The area is the parallel sides added, times the height, divided by two.
teori.geo.trapezoid.4: Common mistake: multiplying all three numbers. Add the parallel sides first.
teori.geo.trapezoid.5: Try it: a = 2, b = 6 and h = 5. What is the area?
teori.geo.compositeCircle.1: Here is a square with a round hole. The coloured part is the square minus the circle.
teori.geo.compositeCircle.2: The square: 6 · 6 = 36. The circle's diameter is 6, so the radius is 3: 3,14 · 3 · 3 = 3,14 · 9 = 28,26.
teori.geo.compositeCircle.3: Take the hole away: 36 − 28,26 = 7,74. Rounded: 7,7 cm².
teori.geo.compositeCircle.4: Common mistake: using the side 6 as the radius. The circle's radius is half the side.
teori.geo.compositeCircle.5: Try it: what is the area of a half circle with radius 2?
teori.geo.inverseArea.1: Sometimes you know the area but not a side. Then you work backwards.
teori.geo.inverseArea.2: Write the formula with the unknown: 6 · h = 24. Divide both sides by 6: h = 4 cm.
teori.geo.inverseArea.3: A square with area 49 cm²: the side is the square root of 49, so 7 cm.
teori.geo.inverseArea.4: Common mistake: multiplying instead of dividing.
teori.geo.inverseArea.5: Try it: a triangle has base 8 and area 20. How high is it?
teori.geo.sector.1: A sector is a slice of the circle, like a slice of cake. The angle v says how big the slice is.
teori.geo.sector.2: A sector is v/360 of the whole circle – of both the area and the arc round the edge.
teori.geo.sector.3: 90° is a quarter of 360°. The whole circle: 3,14 · 4 · 4 = 3,14 · 16 = 50,24. A quarter: 50,24 / 4 = 12,56 – about 12,6 cm².
teori.geo.sector.4: Common mistake: dividing by 100. A full turn is 360°.
teori.geo.sector.5: Try it: what is a sector of 180°?
teori.geo.areaSine.1: If you know two sides and the angle between them, you can find the area without the height.
teori.geo.areaSine.2: The area rule: T = a · b · sin C / 2, where C is the angle between a and b.
teori.geo.areaSine.4: Common mistake: forgetting sin C. a · b / 2 only works when the angle is a right angle.
adv.prompt.expand: Expand the expression – write it without brackets.
adv.prompt.factor: Factorise the expression – write it as a product.
adv.prompt.squareTrick: Work it out with the squaring rule.
adv.prompt.conjugateTrick: Work it out with the conjugate rule.
adv.tip.3.3.4: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². Don't forget the double product 2ab!
adv.tip.3.3.5: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². Backwards: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
adv.tip.3.3.6: x² = c has two solutions: ±√c. If x is in every term, take x out. A product is 0 when one of its factors is 0.
expr.expandFurther: The right expression – but expand it all the way, without brackets.
expr.factorFurther: The right expression – but write it as a product, with brackets.
teori.adv.squareRules.1: (a + b)² is a square with side a + b. It is made of an a² square, a b² square and two ab rectangles.
teori.adv.squareRules.2: So (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². With minus, the middle term is negative: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
teori.adv.squareRules.4: The rule is a mental maths trick too: 31² = (30 + 1)² = 900 + 60 + 1 = 961.
teori.adv.squareRules.5: Common mistake: forgetting the double product. (x + 3)² is not x² + 9.
teori.adv.conjugateRule.1: The conjugate rule: the sum times the difference of the same two numbers is the difference of their squares.
teori.adv.conjugateRule.2: Multiply it out to see why: the middle terms −ab and +ab cancel.
teori.adv.conjugateRule.3: Backwards, you can factorise: x² − 49 = x² − 7² = (x + 7)(x − 7).
teori.adv.conjugateRule.5: Common mistake: expecting a middle term. (x + 4)(x − 4) = x² − 16, nothing else.
teori.adv.quadraticBasics.1: x² = 25 has two solutions: both 5 and −5 squared make 25. Write x = ±5.
teori.adv.quadraticBasics.2: If there is a number in front of x², divide first: 3x² = 48 gives x² = 16, so x = ±4.
teori.adv.quadraticBasics.3: If x is in every term, take x out: x² − 6x = 0 becomes x(x − 6) = 0.
teori.adv.quadraticBasics.4: A product is 0 when one of its factors is 0 – the zero product rule. Each factor gives a solution.
teori.adv.quadraticBasics.5: Common mistake: forgetting the negative solution. x² = 25 has two solutions.
teori.adv.quadraticBasics.6: Try it: what are the solutions of x² + 4x = 0?
teori.adv.pq.6: Is the equation not in the form x² + px + q = 0? Move everything to the left side and divide by the number in front of x² first.
teori.basic.timesTables.1: 3 plates with 4 cookies on each. How many cookies is that?
teori.basic.timesTables.2: You can add: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The shorter way is times: 3 · 4 = 12.
teori.basic.timesTables.3: The order doesn't matter: 3 · 4 is the same as 4 · 3. Know one and you know the other!
teori.basic.timesTables.4: Common mistake: adding instead of multiplying. 3 · 4 isn't 7.
teori.basic.divisionFacts.1: 12 cookies are shared equally between 3 animals. Each gets 4. It's written 12 / 3 = 4.
teori.basic.divisionFacts.2: Division is the times table backwards: which number times 3 makes 12? It's 4.
teori.basic.divisionFacts.3: Common mistake: taking away. 12 / 3 isn't 9 – you share it into 3 equal parts.
teori.basic.missingNumber.1: The scale is level: the box and 7 weigh as much as 15. What does the box weigh?
teori.basic.missingNumber.2: Count backwards: 15 − 7 = 8. The missing number is 8.
teori.basic.missingNumber.4: Common mistake: adding the numbers that are there. 15 + 7 = 22 – but 22 + 7 isn't 15.
teori.basic.missingNumber.5: Which number goes in the box?
teori.basic.clock.1: A clock has two hands. The short one shows the hour, the long one the minutes. Here the long hand points at 12 and the short one at 3: it's 3.00.
teori.basic.clock.2: The long hand at 6 is 30 minutes – half a turn. It's 3.30, half past three.
teori.basic.clock.3: For the long hand each number is 5 minutes. At 3 it's 3 · 5 = 15 minutes: it's 3.15, quarter past three.
teori.basic.clock.4: At 9 it's 9 · 5 = 45 minutes: it's 3.45, quarter to four.
teori.basic.clock.5: Common mistake: misreading the short hand. At 3.30 it's halfway between 3 and 4 – it's still 3 until the long hand reaches 12.
teori.basic.clock.faces: Clocks look different. Some have Roman numerals (III is 3, IX is 9), some only 12, 3, 6 and 9, and some no numbers at all – then you count the ticks. The hands work the same way.
teori.basic.clock.digital: A digital clock shows numbers. After 12 it keeps counting: 13 is 1 in the afternoon, 15 is 3. 15:30 is half past three in the afternoon.
teori.basic.duration.1: How long is it from 9.40 to 11.15? Count in three steps.
teori.basic.duration.2: First to the whole hour: from 9.40 to 10.00 is 20 minutes.
teori.basic.duration.3: Then whole hours: from 10.00 to 11.00 is 60 minutes.
teori.basic.duration.4: Last the rest: from 11.00 to 11.15 is 15 minutes. Altogether: 20 + 60 + 15 = 95 minutes.
teori.basic.duration.5: Common mistake: working with the times as decimals. An hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
teori.basic.duration.6: How many minutes is it from 10.30 to 11.15?
teori.basic.money.1: In the wallet there's 50 kr, 20 kr, 10 kr, 5 kr, 2 kr and 1 kr. How much is that?
teori.basic.money.2: Start with the notes: 50 + 20 + 10 = 80. Then add the coins: 80 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 88 kr.
teori.basic.money.3: Common mistake: counting how many notes and coins there are. It's the kronor that are added up.
teori.basic.money.4: How many kronor are 20 kr, 20 kr, 5 kr and 1 kr?
teori.basic.shapeCount.1: A cube is drawn like this: the dashed edges are the ones you can't see, at the back.
teori.basic.shapeCount.2: The corners: 4 at the front and 4 at the back – 8 corners.
teori.basic.shapeCount.3: The edges: 4 at the front, 4 at the back and 4 going between – 12 edges.
teori.basic.shapeCount.4: Common mistake: forgetting the dashed edges. They're there, even though you can't see them.
teori.basic.shapeCount.5: How many faces does a cuboid have?
teori.basic.angles.1: A right angle is 90° – the corner of a sheet of paper. A straight angle is 180° – a straight line. A full turn is 360°.
teori.basic.angles.2: The angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. Here two of them are 60° and 70°.
teori.basic.angles.3: Add the ones you know: 60 + 70 = 130. Take it away from 180: x = 50°.
teori.basic.angles.4: Common mistake: taking it away from 360. That's for a quadrilateral – a triangle has 180°.
teori.basic.angles.5: A triangle has the angles 40° and 90°. How big is the third?
teori.basic.coordinates.1: A coordinate system has an x-axis going right and a y-axis going up. The point A is 3 to the right and 2 up.
teori.basic.coordinates.2: It's written A = (3, 2). First x – to the right – then y – up.
teori.basic.coordinates.3: Common mistake: swapping the numbers. (2, 3) is a different point: 2 to the right and 3 up.
teori.basic.equationsYoung.1: A balance scale, level: both sides weigh the same. On one side are x and 7, on the other 15. How much does x weigh? It's written x + 7 = 15.
teori.basic.equationsYoung.2: Do the opposite: it says plus 7, so take away 7. x = 15 − 7 = 8.
teori.basic.equationsYoung.3: 4x means 4 times x. It says times, so divide: x = 28 / 4 = 7.
teori.basic.equationsYoung.4: Common mistake: taking away when it says times. 4x = 28 – divide by 4, don't take away 4.
teori.basic.primes.1: A prime can only be divided evenly by 1 and by itself. The first ones are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 …
teori.basic.primes.2: 21 isn't a prime, because 21 = 3 · 7. Try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7.
teori.basic.primes.3: Every number can be split into primes. Divide by the smallest prime that works, again and again: 60 = 2 · 2 · 3 · 5.
teori.basic.primes.4: Common mistake: thinking 1 is a prime. A prime has exactly two divisors – 1 has only one.
teori.basic.primes.5: Which of the numbers is a prime?
teori.basic.estimation.1: An estimate is a quick calculation with round numbers, so you know roughly what the answer is. 49 · 21 ≈ 50 · 20 = 1000.
teori.basic.estimation.2: Big numbers are rounded to hundreds: 398 + 207 ≈ 400 + 200 = 600.
teori.basic.estimation.3: Common mistake: rounding the wrong way. 49 is closest to 50, not 40.
teori.basic.areaUnits.1: 1 dm is 10 cm. A square with side 1 dm holds 10 · 10 = 100 squares of 1 cm². So 1 dm² = 100 cm².
teori.basic.areaUnits.2: Each step between mm², cm², dm² and m² is 100 times.
teori.basic.areaUnits.3: To a smaller unit there are more: 3 dm² = 3 · 100 = 300 cm².
teori.basic.areaUnits.4: Common mistake: thinking it's 10 times, as for lengths. For area it's 100.
teori.basic.shopPay.1: Swedish money: coins of 1, 2, 5 and 10 kronor, and notes of 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500 kronor.
teori.basic.shopPay.2: An ice cream costs 37 kr. First take the biggest that isn't too much: a 20 note. Then 10, 5 and 2.
teori.basic.shopPay.4: Common mistake: counting how many coins there are. A 50 note is just one note – but it's worth 50 kronor.
teori.basic.shopChange.1: Now you work at the till. A customer buys an ice cream for 37 kr and pays with a 50 note. How much should they get back?
teori.basic.shopChange.2: Count up from the price: from 37 to 40 is 3 kr.
teori.basic.shopChange.3: From 40 to 50 is 10 kr. Altogether 3 + 10 = 13 kr.
teori.basic.shopChange.4: Give back 13 kr – for example a 10-krona, a 2-krona and a 1-krona coin.
teori.basic.shopChange.5: Common mistake: adding the price and the note. The change is the difference: 50 − 37 = 13.
teori.basic.shopChange.6: Something costs 64 kr and the customer pays with 100 kr. How much change?
expr.checkNumber: Check the number {n} (in red) – it isn't in the question, and you didn't work it out. Did you use the right measurement?
basic.tip.1.4.2: Division is the times table backwards: which number times 3 makes 12?
basic.tip.1.4.3: Count backwards: what's missing in an addition you find with minus.
basic.tip.1.5.1: The short hand shows the hour, the long hand the minutes. Each number is 5 minutes for the long hand.
basic.tip.1.5.2: First count to the whole hour, then whole hours, then the minutes left over.
basic.tip.1.6.1: Start with the biggest notes and coins, and add the smaller ones.
basic.tip.1.2.2: Count one at a time, and put a finger on each so you don't count anything twice.
basic.tip.2.12.1: A right angle is 90°, a straight angle 180°, a full turn 360°. A triangle's angles add up to 180°, a quadrilateral's to 360°.
basic.tip.2.13.1: First x – how far right – then y – how far up.
basic.tip.2.14.1: Do the opposite: if it says plus, take away. If it says times, divide.
basic.tip.2.15.1: A prime can only be divided evenly by 1 and itself. Try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7.
basic.tip.2.10.3: Round the numbers first – to tens or hundreds – then work it out with the round numbers.
basic.tip.2.9.4: Between mm², cm², dm² and m² it's 100 times, not 10.
basic.tip.2.9.5: Count to the whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest. An hour is 60 minutes.

clock.label: A clock with hands
clock.readShown: It is {time}: the long hand is {minute}, and the short one {hour}.
clock.readWrongMinute: Look at the long hand – it is {where}.
clock.readWrongHour: The minutes are right! Look at the short hand – it is {where}.
clock.toDigital: Set the digital clock to the same time as the clock with hands.
clock.toDigital24: It is afternoon or evening. Set the digital clock to the same time – after 12 it keeps counting: 13, 14, 15 …
clock.digitalHint: Drag the numbers up or down – or tap the arrows.
clock.digitalShown: This is how it should look: {time}.
clock.digitalWrongMinute: The minutes aren't right. Look at the long hand.
clock.digitalWrongHour: The minutes are right! But not the hours – look at the short hand, it is {where}.
clock.digitalWrongHour24: The minutes are right! But not the hours. The short hand is {where} – and it's afternoon, so add 12.
clock.setDigital: Set the clock with hands to the same time as the digital clock.
clock.setDigital24: Set the clock with hands to the same time. Remember: a clock with hands only has 1–12.
clock.dragHint5: Drag the hands. The long one stops at every five minutes.
clock.dragHint1: Drag the hands. The long one stops at every minute – count the ticks.
clock.right: Right! The clock is set right.
clock.shown: This is how it should be: the long hand {minute}, and the short one {hour}.
clock.wrongMinute: The long hand – the minute hand – isn't right. Try again.
clock.wrongHour: The minute hand is right! But the short hand – the hour hand – isn't.
clock.tip: Set the long hand first – it shows the minutes. The short one shows the hour, and it moves a little at a time between the numbers.
clock.tip24: {h} on a digital clock is {twelve} on a clock with hands (12 less).
clock.hourNear: just past {h} – on its way to {n}
clock.hourNearNext: more than halfway from {h} to {n} – close to {n}
clock.tip.1.5.1: O'clock: the long hand points straight up at 12. Half past: it points straight down at 6 – and the short hand is halfway between two numbers.
clock.tip.1.5.3: Quarter past: the long hand at 3. Quarter to: the long hand at 9.
clock.tip.1.5.4: Each number is 5 minutes for the long hand: at 4 it's 4 · 5 = 20 minutes.
clock.tip.1.5.5: A digital clock shows hours and minutes in numbers: 7.25 is 25 minutes past 7.
clock.tip.1.5.6: After 12 the digital clock keeps counting: 13 is 1, 18 is 6. Take away 12 to get the hour on a clock with hands.
clock.tip.1.5.7: Count the fives up to the number before, then the small ticks: 4 · 5 + 3 = 23 minutes.
